title: Trees and the BST rule
summary: Name the parts of a tree, and tell a valid BST from a tree that only looks like one.

hook.goal: Name the parts of a tree, and use the BST rule to decide whether a tree is a binary search tree.

scenario.title: Folders inside folders
scenario.text: On your laptop a folder can hold other folders, and those can hold more folders. You have already used a tree.
scenario.recall: A linked-list node has one "next" reference. What if a node had two?

warmUp.question: A linked-list node points to one next node. If every node could point to two nodes, what shape could you build?

options.reply: A chain only needs one reference. With two, a node can split into two branches.

options.text: A branching shape, like folders inside folders
options.reply: Yes. Each node can branch into a left and a right part. That shape is a binary tree.

options.text: A list that is sorted automatically
options.reply: Two references do not sort anything by themselves. The shape is what changes: each node can branch.

hook.bridge: You also met binary search, where one comparison throws away half of the values. Keep that in mind: the BST rule is what lets a tree do the same.

explore.prompt: Predict: in which tree can a search always decide to go left or right at each node?
explore.reveal: Tree A. In B, 40 sits in 50's right subtree although it is smaller than 50. In C, the larger key is on the left.

explore.prompt: What rule did the good tree follow?

options.text: Smaller keys on the left and larger keys on the right, at every node
options.reply: That is the BST rule, which you will see written out next.

options.text: Every node has exactly two children
options.reply: Not quite: in tree A some nodes have no children. Look at where the smaller keys sit.

options.text: The largest key is at the root
options.reply: Not quite: 50 is at the root of A, and 80 is larger. Look at where the smaller keys sit.

pages.note: Binary means each node has at most two children, called left and right.
pages.caption: Depth of 40 is 2 (two highlighted edges). Tree T has height 2.

pages.title: The BST rule
steps: For every node, every key in its left subtree is smaller than the node.
Every key in its right subtree is larger than the node.
The rule covers the whole subtree, not just the children.
An empty tree is a BST.
pages.caption: Everything under 30 is smaller than 50. Everything under 70 is larger than 50.

steps.text: 50 has no parent, so 50 is the root.
20, 40, 60 and 80 have no children, so they are leaves.
The depth of 40 is 2: there are two edges from the root to 40.
The subtree rooted at 30 has height 1: the longest path down from 30 has one edge.
Tree T has height 2: the longest path from the root to a leaf has two edges.
Check 50. Its left subtree holds 30, which is smaller than 50. That side is fine.
Its right subtree holds 70 and 40. Every key there must be larger than 50.
40 is smaller than 50 but sits in 50's right subtree. The rule is broken at 40.
Next to its parent 70, 40 looks fine. That is why checking only parent and child is not enough. X is not a BST.

steps.prompt: Put the label "root" on the tree: click the root.
steps.right: 50 has no parent, so it is the root.
steps.wrong: The root is the one node with no parent.

steps.prompt: Now label a leaf: click any leaf.
steps.right: Correct: that node has no children.
steps.wrong: A leaf has no children. Look along the bottom row.

steps.right: 30 is directly above 40, so it is 40's parent.
steps.wrong: The parent is the node directly above 40.

steps.prompt: There is an empty spot on the right of 60. Which key could go there?
steps.right: 65 fits: it is larger than 60 and smaller than 70.
steps.wrong: Check every ancestor: the spot is in 50's right subtree, in 70's left subtree, and on 60's right.

items.prompt: Click the root and every leaf of this tree.

hints.text: The root has no parent. A leaf has no children. How many of each can you find?
The nodes with no children are now outlined. Remember the root as well.

items.explanation: The root is {root}. The leaves are {leaves}, because they have no children.

items.prompt: Give the depth of {40} and the height of the subtree rooted at {30}.

hints.text: Depth counts edges from the root. Height counts edges on the longest path down to a leaf.
The edges from the root to {40} are highlighted, and the subtree rooted at {30} is outlined. Count edges, not nodes.

items.explanation: The depth of {40} is 2: two edges from the root. The subtree rooted at {30} has height 1: one edge down to a leaf.
items.misconception: Mixing up depth and height, or counting nodes instead of edges.

items.prompt: Is this tree a valid BST?

hints.text: For every node: are all keys on its left smaller, and all keys on its right larger?
The left subtree of the root is outlined. Is every key there smaller than {50}?

items.explanation: Valid. At every node, every key in the left subtree is smaller and every key in the right subtree is larger.

items.prompt: Is this tree a valid BST? If not, click the node that breaks the rule.

hints.text: Compare each node with every ancestor, not only with its parent.
Everything in {50}'s right subtree (outlined) must be larger than {50}. Which node does not fit?

items.explanation: Invalid. {40} is in the right subtree of {50} but is smaller than {50}, even though it sits correctly under its parent {70}.
items.misconception: Checking a node only against its parent.

items.prompt: Is this tree a valid BST? If not, click the node that breaks the rule.

hints.text: Compare each node with every ancestor, not only with its parent.
Every key in {50}'s left subtree must be smaller than {50}, so the spot right of {30} only allows keys from {31} to {49}.

items.explanation: Invalid. {55} is larger than {50} but sits on {50}'s left side.
items.misconception: Checking a node only against its parent.

items.prompt: True or false: checking each parent against its own children is enough to know a tree is a BST.

hints.text: Think back to tree X. Did every parent-child pair look fine?
Here {55} is fine next to its parent {30}. Now compare it with the root.

items.explanation: False. A key must be on the correct side of every ancestor, not only its parent.
items.misconception: Checking a node only against its parent.
